Formulation
- Brief summary:
  - A previously well 19-year-old female student with acute onset (several days) of dysuria, lower abdominal cramping and intermittent visible blood in urine. Sexual activity with condom use and no prior STI screening reported. Past IBS is noted. Clinical features are most consistent with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. Predisposing factors: female sex and sexual activity. Precipitating factor: acute infectious symptoms over several days. Perpetuating factors: delay of a few days before seeking care; lack of prior STI screening. Protective factors: generally well, social supports, engaged with care. Allergy to clindamycin noted, which will influence antibiotic choices.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Suspected uncomplicated urinary tract infection (dysuria, lower abdominal cramp, intermittent hematuria)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Relief of pain and urinary symptoms; return to usual health.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Treat suspected UTI effectively; prevent progression to upper urinary tract infection; monitor for complications.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Start prescribed antibiotic as advised (one tablet twice daily for three days — agent to be either nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; strength not documented).
  - Increase fluid intake to help flush the urinary tract.
  - Consider cranberry juice as adjunctive symptomatic measure (patient advised that it can sometimes help symptoms).
  - Avoid sexual intercourse while symptomatic if possible; continue barrier contraception (condoms) if sexually active.
  - Seek follow-up if symptoms worsen (fever, back/flank pain, increased unwellness) or if still unwell by end of the week.
  - Consider pregnancy test if concerned about pregnancy (advised by clinician).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide antibiotic prescription (either nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; regimen discussed as one tablet twice daily for three days; specific agent and dose/strength to be documented on prescription).
  - Advise increased oral fluids and symptomatic measures.
  - Advise avoidance of sexual activity until symptoms resolve; continue barrier contraception.
  - Provide safety-netting instructions: patient to contact/return if fever, back pain, worsening symptoms, or if no improvement by end of week.

Secondary Problem: Sexual/reproductive health screening (no prior STI screening; contraception: condoms)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Ensure appropriate STI screening and reproductive health reassurance if required.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Arrange appropriate STI screening if indicated; rule out pregnancy if clinically necessary.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Consider scheduling an STI screen (patient reported never having had one).
  - Perform pregnancy test if concerned or if clinician advises.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Offer or arrange STI screening/testing as appropriate (not documented that this was completed during consult).
  - Document pregnancy test if performed; advise on sexual health follow-up.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of likely UTI, antibiotic treatment options (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim) and a three-day regimen described, importance of fluids, symptomatic measures (cranberry juice), avoidance of sexual activity while symptomatic, warning signs of worsening infection (fever, back pain, systemic unwellness), and instruction to return if no improvement by end of week.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - High temperature/fever, back/flank pain, generally feeling more unwell, persistent or worsening urinary symptoms, lack of improvement by end of week.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Increase fluids, rest, symptomatic measures (as above), seek timely medical review if symptoms worsen.
